show.description: This psychological thriller based on Stephen King's novel Misery follows successful romance novelist Paul Sheldon, who is rescued from a car crash and wakes up captive in a secluded home owned by his self-identified "number one fan," Annie Wilkes. show.title: Steel Magnolias
show.author: Robert Harling
show.description: Set in Truvy Jones's beauty salon in Chinquapin, Louisiana, the gathering place for the town's women, the play opens as Truvy takes on Annelle Dupuy, a timid newcomer still finding her footing. Regulars include Shelby Eatenton, a young nurse getting ready for her wedding; her mother M'Lynn, a mental health counselor; Clairee Belcher, a sharp, well-off widow; and Ouiser Boudreaux, the town's resident grouch. Through gossip, jokes and heart-to-heart talks across several seasons, the women share happiness and hardship, including the tension caused by Shelby's wish to have children despite the risks of her Type 1 diabetes. The title captures their nature: delicate as magnolias but as tough as steel, in a story that celebrates female friendship while facing love, loss and community.

roles.notes: Stage age 40s to early 60s. Owner of the beauty salon; quick-witted, kind and funny. Uses hair and beauty to connect with people, has never met a stranger, and keeps her shop warm and welcoming while handing out advice and humor.

Stage age late teens to mid-20s. A young beauty-school graduate, new to town and unsure about her personal life and marriage. Shy at first, she gains confidence and her own voice as she becomes part of the salon community.

Stage age late 40s to early 60s. Shelby's mother; smart, intuitive and compassionate, the emotional anchor of her family and community. Balances protecting her daughter with empowering her, and shows resilience and deep maternal love through Shelby's risky pregnancy.

Stage age 20s. M'Lynn's daughter; strong-willed, determined, outgoing and caring, often a caregiver herself despite the limits of her Type 1 diabetes. Her health and her drive to live fully shape much of the play's emotional arc.
Stage age 50s to early 80s. Widow of the former mayor; classy, sharp-tongued and funny. Loves teasing her friends but is deeply supportive as she discovers independence after her husband's death.
Stage age 50s to early 80s. A wealthy, eccentric curmudgeon; blunt, sarcastic and critical of convention, yet fiercely loyal and loving. Brings both comic relief and emotional depth to the group.

show.description: In Ivan Menchell's comedy, three Jewish widows get together every month for tea before visiting their husbands' graves, until a widower named Sam upsets the routine and tests their loyalties. Ida is ready for a new beginning, Lucille wants fun and attention, and Doris holds tight to tradition. As Sam's interest in Ida shakes up the group, each woman has to face what it means to love, to let go, and to live fully again, in a story that mixes humor and tenderness while dealing with grief, friendship and the fear of moving on.

roles.notes: Female, 60s+. Sweet-tempered, warm and quietly resilient; learning to live after losing her husband of 39 years. The emotional anchor and peacemaker of her group, she slowly opens up to the possibility of new love. Needs emotional depth, natural warmth, subtle comic timing, and light physical comedy including a bit of cha-cha dancing.

Female, 60s+. Feisty, flirtatious and full of life; after learning her late husband Harry was unfaithful, she throws herself back into dating out of revenge, loneliness and a refusal to grieve forever. Outspoken and larger than life, with many of the show's biggest laughs through physical comedy, cha-cha dancing and mishaps; needs strong comic timing, high energy and the hidden vulnerability of a broken heart.

Female, 60s+. Practical, proper and devoted to the memory of her late husband, Abe; sharp-tongued, judgmental and horrified when her friends start dating. Beneath the rigid surface is a woman struggling with grief, loneliness and fear of change. Provides conflict and comedy through outspoken opinions, physical comedy and cha-cha dancing; needs strong comic instincts and heartfelt humanity.

Male, 60s+. A widowed local butcher with a kind heart; shy, sincere and quietly charming. Meeting Ida while visiting his late wife's grave, he forms a tender bond with her and grounds the women's lively personalities. Needs quiet strength, genuine vulnerability and understated humor for a believable romance.

Female, 40s-60s. Confident, pleasant and unaware of the stir she causes; appears briefly as Sam's date to a wedding, sparking jealousy and emotional upheaval among the widows. A smaller but important role needing warmth, poise and natural charm.

show.description: Ken Ludwig's madcap farce, in the spirit of his Lend Me a Tenor, follows George and Charlotte Hay, a pair of fading 1950s stage stars touring Private Lives and Cyrano de Bergerac in repertory in Buffalo, New York, with a company of just five actors. With their marriage about to blow apart over George's fling with a young ingenue, they learn they may have one final shot at fame: Frank Capra is coming to see their matinee and could cast them in his film remake of The Scarlet Pimpernel. Naturally, everything that can go wrong does, helped along by their daughter's hopelessly clueless fiancé and by mounting confusion over which play is actually being performed, thanks to Charlotte's deaf, elderly stage-manager mother, who despises George. Directed by Mary Ross at Theatre of Dare in Kitty Hawk.

show.title: A Year with Frog and Toad
show.author: Willie Reale (book & lyrics)
show.description: Drawn from Arnold Lobel's beloved books and set to a catchy score by Robert and Willie Reale, this whimsical musical follows two devoted friends, cheerful, well-liked Frog and the rather grumpy Toad, through four lively seasons. After waking from hibernation in the spring, the pair plant gardens, go swimming, rake leaves and go sledding, picking up life lessons along the way and celebrating the differences that make each of them special. Part vaudeville and part make-believe, and full of charm, it is the story of a friendship that lasts all year round. Directed by Vivian Stem and Kim Plyler at Theatre of Dare in Kitty Hawk.

show.title: Marjorie Prime
show.author: Jordan Harrison
show.description: Set in an age of artificial intelligence, Jordan Harrison's play centers on Marjorie, an 85-year-old woman whose memories have become scattered and are slipping away, and the handsome new companion she has been given: a "Prime" programmed to tell the story of her own life back to her. The play asks what we would choose to hold onto, and what we would let go of, if the choice were ours, and through spare, quietly wondrous storytelling it probes the nature of human identity and whether there is anything technology cannot stand in for. Directed by Tim Hass, this four-person, 80-minute play is performed at Dare Arts in Manteo.

requirements.additionalNotes: Auditions are Saturday, January 23 and Sunday, January 24, 2027, at 6:00 PM, upstairs at Dare Arts, 300 Queen Elizabeth Avenue, Manteo. This is a four-person, 80-minute play, so actors need to be able to learn lines quickly. The casting team is looking for subtle emotional truth rather than big theatricality: lean into the emotional undercurrent of each character instead of surface traits, since the play is quiet, intimate, intelligent and deeply human. The website does not list a specific audition format or materials. Performances are March 12, 13, 18, 19 and 20 at 7:30 PM and March 14 and 21 at 2:00 PM at Dare Arts; individual tickets go on sale February 19. Directed by Tim Hass.

roles.notes: Female, 60-90 (plays her 80s). Elegant and quick-witted but fading; living with memory loss, though her old brilliance keeps flashing through. Funny, flirtatious, stubborn, vulnerable and very lonely, she wants dignity and connection even as her hold on reality slips. Needs emotional nuance, warmth, and the ability to move quickly between clarity and confusion.

Male, late 20s to early 40s (plays 35). An AI "Prime" recreation of Marjorie's late husband: attentive, calm, patient and almost impossibly kind. He learns by listening and adapting, so he seems human yet slightly incomplete; the actor should balance warmth with a subtle artificial precision.

Female, 40s-60s (plays 55). Marjorie's daughter: practical, emotionally guarded and worn out from years of caregiving, carrying unresolved grief and resentment under a controlled surface. She wrestles with memory, truth and her complicated bond with her mother; the role calls for restraint, with much of her pain held in rather than shown.

Male, 40s-60s (plays 55). Tess's husband: warm, empathetic and emotionally open in ways Tess often is not. He mediates and cares for the family, trying to keep the peace amid emotional fractures, while also grappling with loss and uncertainty himself; grounded and humane but not simple.

show.title: Little Women
show.author: Allan Knee (book)
show.description: Opera House Theatre Company is casting Little Women, the second production of its 2027 season (its 42nd), which plays the Historic Main Stage at Thalian Hall February 18-28, 2027. The musical adapts Louisa May Alcott's classic novel about the four March sisters, following their adventures, both real and imagined, along with heartbreak and a deep sense of hope, as their struggle to find their own voices echoes the growing pains of a young America. Morganna Bridgers directs, with music direction by Bryan Underwood and choreography by Victoria Bartels Prince.

requirements.callbacks: Held immediately after the initial vocal auditions on November 30; those invited are told during their audition. Callbacks include scene readings and vocal selections from the show, and callback materials will be posted on the auditions page.
requirements.additionalNotes: Auditions for Little Women are Monday, November 30, 2026 at 6:00 PM at Opera House Theatre Company's Lucille Shuffler Center, 2011 Carolina Beach Road, Wilmington, NC 28401. Prepare 16-32 bars of a musical theatre song in the style of Little Women that shows off your voice and storytelling; it does not have to be from the show, and you should choose material that lets you make clear acting choices. An accompanist is provided: bring legible sheet music in your key, with the start and end of your cut clearly marked, organized in a binder. You may be stopped before the end of your cut to keep things on schedule; this is not a reflection of your audition. Callbacks follow immediately after the vocal auditions, with scene readings and vocal selections from the show, and invitations are given during your audition. Submit the audition form (Google Form linked on https://www.operahousetheatrecompany.org/auditions) in advance; the character breakdown is linked on the same page. Performers of all races and ethnicities are encouraged to audition for all roles. Jo, Meg, Amy, Laurie and John Brooke must be 18 or older, Professor Bhaer in his mid-20s or older, and Beth may be played by a performer under 18. Rehearsals begin around January 16, 2027, tech week is February 15-18, and performances are February 18-28 at Thalian Hall. Directed by Morganna Bridgers. Questions: mmbridgers@gmail.com.

roles.notes: Female, performer age 18+. An aspiring writer with a restless imagination, quick wit and fierce loyalty to her sisters, who longs for adventure and independence and pushes against what is expected of young women. Impulsive, stubborn and deeply tender under the bravado, she must learn to embrace change without losing herself; needs an actor who can balance bold comedy with emotional vulnerability. Vocal range E3-A5.

Male, performer age mid-20s+, playing age early to mid-30s. A German professor at Mrs. Kirk's New York boarding house: thoughtful, principled and initially reserved, he values honesty and takes Jo's writing seriously enough to challenge her; his formal manner hides warmth, dry humor and loneliness. German dialect required. Vocal range G2-F#4.

Female, performer age 18+. The youngest sister: artistic, ambitious and determined to be taken seriously, sometimes vain or imperious but keenly aware of being left behind; grows into a poised woman with her own convictions. Needs strong comic instincts and the ability to show significant maturation. May double as the Troll. Vocal range Cb4-Gb5.

Female, performer age 18+. The eldest sister: warm, romantic and conscious of setting an example, drawn to beauty, comfort and an elegant life, with a playful spirit and a capacity for steady love; learns what she values and finds the confidence to choose her own happiness. May double as Clarissa. Vocal range A#3-Gb5.

Female, performer age flexible (performers under 18 may be considered). Gentle, observant and happiest at the piano or among loved ones; she avoids the spotlight but has humor, conviction and emotional strength, a close bond with Jo and an unexpected friendship with Mr. Laurence through music. May double as Rodrigo II. Vocal range A3-G5.

Female, playing age mature adult. The sisters' mother, holding the household together while her husband is at war; compassionate, resourceful and principled, carrying loneliness, fear and grief alongside warmth and humor. May double as the Hag. Vocal range Eb3-Eb5.

Male, performer age 18+. The Marches' charming, spirited young neighbor, raised in his grandfather's formal household and drawn to the sisters' warmth and imagination; playful, impulsive and romantic, especially toward Jo, he matures and finds an unexpected partner in Amy. Vocal range Bb2-Bb4.

Female, playing age mature adult. The sisters' wealthy, formidable great-aunt: sharp-tongued, exacting and used to obedience, she believes good manners and good marriages give women security, and clashes especially with Jo; affection lies beneath the criticism. Needs commanding presence, precise comic timing and glimpses of warmth. May double as Mrs. Kirk. Vocal range E3-F5.

Male, performer age 18+. Laurie's conscientious tutor, whose formality can make him seem stiff or awkward; sincere, honorable and quietly affectionate, he finds duty easier than feelings, and his relationship with Meg reveals tenderness and courage. Gentle comedy and romantic warmth. Vocal range C#3-F#4.

Male, playing age older adult (reads as Laurie's grandfather). Laurie's wealthy grandfather and the Marches' imposing neighbor, seemingly stern and impatient; his friendship with Beth and their shared love of music reveal a playful, generous side. Needs a formidable exterior balanced with humor and openness. Vocal range D3-E4.

show.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
show.description: Set in the American South during the Great Depression, To Kill a Mockingbird looks at courage, compassion, justice and the loss of innocence through the eyes of young Scout Finch as her father, Atticus, defends a man falsely accused of a crime. Theatre Statesville says the production offers challenging and rewarding roles for actors of many ages and experience levels.

requirements.additionalNotes: Auditions are Sunday, January 3 and Monday, January 4, 2027 at 7:00 PM at First Presbyterian Church of Statesville, 125 N. Meeting St., Statesville. You only need to attend one night; arrive 15 minutes early to fill out audition forms and plan to stay until the end or until dismissed. Auditions are cold readings from sides provided in advance (https://go.fliplink.me/view/FC37EBBC-F865-410D-949F-BDD8804EEA81); they need not be memorized, but director Dalton Isaac is emphasizing emotion and characterization. Headshots and resumes are welcome but not required, and rehearsal conflicts must be listed on the audition form. All roles are open, and Theatre Statesville casts without regard to age, ethnic or national origin, race, sex, creed, orientation or ability; newcomers are encouraged. This is Christopher Sergel's revised adaptation of Harper Lee's novel, and the script will not be altered: it contains racial slurs and racially charged content, depictions of violence and racism, references to rape and sexual assault, brief gunfire audio and strobe-like lighting. The read-through is Sunday, January 24 at 6:30 PM, with rehearsals mostly Wednesday and Sunday evenings at 6:30 PM and Saturdays at 11:00 AM, plus more evenings in late February and March; no conflicts are allowed from March 13 onward (load-in March 20, tech March 21-24). Performances are March 25, 26, 27 and April 1, 2, 3 at 7:30 PM and March 28 and April 4 at 2:30 PM, plus school field-trip performances on March 31 and April 1 that all cast members must be available for (younger cast members get excused school absences). Full audition packet: https://canva.link/mockingbirdauditions . Questions: Artistic Director Dalton Isaac, director@theatrestatesville.com.

roles.notes: Female, 9-12 (ages from the novel; flexible). A girl on the verge of the events that will shape her life; ideally reads as young as nine. Brave and blunt, she asks whatever question comes to mind. Ethnicity: Caucasian.

Male, 13-15. Scout's older brother, reaching out, perhaps even more than she does, to understand their unconventional father; his strongest undercurrent is a wish to connect with Atticus. Ethnicity: Caucasian.
Male, 13-14. Small, blond and wise beyond his years, neater and better dressed than his friends, with a quick, happy laugh; something is missing at home, and he senses it in Atticus. Ethnicity: any.

Male, 40-55. Tall, quietly impressive, reserved and civilized, nearly fifty and bespectacled; gave up shooting because his skill felt like an unfair advantage. Courageous without heroics, he does what he believes is just. Ethnicity: Caucasian.
Female, 30+. Proud, capable and self-educated, she has raised the motherless Scout and Jem with high standards and uncompromising discipline. Ethnicity: African American.
Female, 35-50. Younger than Atticus but of his generation; a lovely, sensitive woman whose wisdom and compassion reflect the South's best instincts. Ethnicity: any.
Female, 35-40. The neighborhood gossip, who relishes it so much it is almost funny; sometimes petty, partly because she cannot resist stirring things up. Ethnicity: any.
Female, 60+. An elderly, ailing woman who walks with difficulty, made biting and bitter by pain, and fighting a private battle that matters to Jem and Scout. Ethnicity: Caucasian.
Male, 35-40. A pale recluse who has not left his house in fifteen years; drawn out only by an emergency, he is unsure with people and eager to retreat once his task is done. Ethnicity: any.

Male, 25-30. Handsome and vital, with a left hand crippled in a childhood accident; married to Helen with young children, he meets a false charge with quiet dignity, kindness and sensitivity. Ethnicity: African American.
Male, 40-60. The town sheriff, a complex man who enforces the law without favor; his true feelings surface in his final speeches to Atticus. Ethnicity: any.
Male, 50+. A wintry Southern judge who does what he can, within his time, to see justice done; he runs his court impartially but sympathizes with Tom. Ethnicity: any.
Male, 40-45. Minister of the First Purchase Church, an imposing man with strong stage presence and a powerful preacher's voice. Ethnicity: African American.

Female, 18-21. A desperately lonely, overworked young woman whose need for companionship overwhelms everything; when her reaching out backfires she fights just as desperately for what she sees as survival. Ethnicity: Caucasian.

Male, 35-50. Mayella's irritable father, living with his large family by the town dump; he expects the trial to make him important, and when Atticus destroys his credibility his rage borders on paranoia. Ethnicity: Caucasian.
Male, 40. A struggling farmer who shares the era's prejudices but can be reached as a human being, and who leads the others away once his attitude changes. Ethnicity: Caucasian.
Male, any age. The public prosecutor, cruel and hurtful in manner, yet privately doubtful of Tom's guilt. Ethnicity: any.
Any gender, any age. Ethnicity: any.

5+ BIPOC actors ages 16 and up and 3+ Caucasian adults of any gender and age for ensemble and background roles; singing ability and experience preferred but not required. Not needed at every rehearsal. You will be asked at auditions whether you would accept a non-speaking role.

roles.notes: A complex, tough and streetwise orphan who is still vulnerable when she fears losing the new family she has come to love; she moves from motherly to independent, overwhelmed, needy and hopeful as the story goes on. show.title: Annie
show.author: Thomas Meehan (book)
show.description: Myrtle Beach ACT's pre-professional Company Theater program stages its winter production: the full-length Broadway musical Annie, performed by young artists ages 8 to 18 who were selected for their developed singing, dancing and acting skills, with MBACT presenting it at the Broadway Theater at Broadway at the Beach. The story follows Annie, a hopeful and gutsy 11-year-old orphan with a big personality, who escapes the grip of Miss Hannigan, the comically cruel woman who runs her orphanage, when she is chosen to spend time in the home of wealthy businessman Oliver Warbucks and his warm, capable secretary Grace Farrell. As Annie wins over Warbucks and his household staff, Miss Hannigan's scheming brother Rooster and his flighty girlfriend Lily St. Regis plot to cash in on her good fortune, while Annie's loyal dog Sandy, her fellow orphans, a radio show, Hooverville citizens, New Yorkers and even President Franklin D. Roosevelt and his cabinet all play a part in her search for a family. MBACT calls it another iconic production for the company.

show.author: William Shakespeare
show.description: Shared Radiance Performing Arts Company and Creative Greensboro are producing William Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors as a youth production. The play is a whirlwind of mistaken identities and long-lost twins. Antipholus of Syracuse and his servant Dromio have traveled the world looking for the family they have never known, and their search finally brings them to Ephesus, a city where anyone from Syracuse is forbidden. They are nearer to finding their missing relatives than they suspect, yet every step closer only multiplies the chaos and confusion, and it is an open question whether the missing pieces of their family will finally fall into place or whether even more will go astray. This staging moves the story to early Hollywood at the peak of slapstick comedy, giving its young theatre makers room to explore physical comedy, ensemble work and plenty of all-around silliness. Male presenting. He directs the play-within-the-play, Murder at Haversham Manor, and plays the respected Inspector Carter. Female presenting. A vain actress with an enormous ego who craves adoration and dreams of Hollywood. She will knock down anyone in her path, but is shrewd enough to stay in the good graces of anyone who can help her, such as the director. The stakes feel huge to her, and the part is very physical.

Male presenting. An actor who models himself on Richard Burton and plays everything outward, though he is not a send-up of a bad actor so much as someone oblivious to those around him. He feels no guilt when things go wrong, never learns from his errors, and is locked in a power struggle with Chris over the presidency of the Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society, which matters enormously to him.

Male presenting. A somewhat bland actor who pictures himself as a James Bond type. He is excited and enjoying himself, cares about the play but mostly for the fun of it, and technically has to keep the show moving. Charles Haversham is an especially physically demanding role.

Male presenting. A first-time actor who has learned his lines and does exactly as he is told, with no real connection to his castmates. Whenever he gets a laugh he breaks the fourth wall to play to the audience. Childlike and naive, his mistakes are basic ones because he never thinks anything through.

Male presenting. He has no real interest in theatre and is mainly there to make friends, believing a good performance will help him socially. Audience laughter feels like agony and personal tragedy to him; he is a little clueless but does realize when he has gotten something wrong.
